q: Three of us recorded a radio play, each in our own bedroom. How do I make it sound like we're all in the same room?
a: 1. Clean each voice first so the bedrooms matter less: Essential Sound ▸ Dialogue ▸ Reduce Noise and Reduce Reverb on each person's clips. 2. Add Audio Submix Track (Sequence menu, `mixer.addSubmix`): S1 appears in the mixer. 3. Put one reverb on S1: `mixer.addInsert` with `effect` `studio_reverb`, and pick a room that fits the scene. 4. On each voice track add a send to S1 (`mixer.addSend`, `target` S1) and set its level (`mixer.setSend`, `levelDb`): the dry voice still goes to the Mix, the send adds the shared room. A little more send makes a voice feel further away. Why one reverb: three clip reverbs give three different rooms; one shared reverb glues the voices into one space. Clip reverbs are still handy for a single line that must sound somewhere else.

q: In Fairlight I send all the dialogue tracks to one reverb bus. What's the equivalent here?
a: A submix is the bus. Add one (`mixer.addSubmix`), put the reverb on it as an insert (`mixer.addInsert`, `effect` `studio_reverb`), then add a send from each dialogue track to it (`mixer.addSend`; `mixer.setSend` sets the level and pre / post fader, `mixer.removeSend` takes it off). Routing a track's whole output to the submix instead (`mixer.setStrip` with `output`) gives one fader for all dialogue, but then everything goes through the reverb, so use sends for a reverb and output routing for a group fader. A submix can feed a later submix, never an earlier one.

q: my podcast guests all sound like different rooms, can i make it one room
a: Take each room out as far as it goes first: Essential Sound ▸ Dialogue ▸ Reduce Reverb (and Reduce Noise) on each guest's clips. Then add a little of one shared room to all of them: a submix (`mixer.addSubmix`) with a Studio Reverb insert (`mixer.addInsert`, a small room at a low level) and a send from each guest track (`mixer.addSend`). Keep it subtle: the aim is that they match, not that it echoes. A very echoey recording won't fully match; the shared room only hides the difference.

q: My voice-over is recorded really close to the mic: the P's pop and the S's hiss. How do I fix it without ruining my voice?
a: 1. Pops: Essential Sound ▸ Dialogue ▸ Reduce Rumble (a High Pass; 3–4 is about 66–78 Hz) removes most of them. For one bad pop, dip the clip's Volume with two quick keyframes over it in Effect Controls, or cut it out and fill with room tone. 2. Esses: DeEss at about 3–6 (it drives the DeEsser). De-ess after any EQ or presence boost, because those bring the esses up. 3. Listen back: too much de-essing makes you lisp, and a high pass set too high (150 Hz and up) thins the voice. Next recording: speak slightly past the mic rather than straight into it.

q: In Premiere I'd put a DeEsser and a High Pass on a close announcer read. Where are those in Revolution?
a: Same names: the DeEsser and High Pass effects, or Essential Sound's Dialogue controls that drive them: Reduce Rumble (High Pass, 30–150 Hz) and DeEss (threshold and reduction together). A usual order: high pass first, then EQ (a preset such as Warm Voice or Presence Lift), then de-ess last, since EQ and compression bring sibilance up. A single plosive is better fixed with a Volume keyframe dip than by raising the high pass for the whole read.

q: my narration sounds harsh and spitty in headphones
a: That's sibilance plus too much top end. In Essential Sound ▸ Dialogue: DeEss around 3–6, and the EQ preset Soften Harshness at a low amount. Raise them slowly and stop when the esses stop jumping out: overdone, the voice lisps or goes dull. If you boosted presence earlier, back it off a little first.

q: I time like a film lab: printer points on the whole reel, a point warmer here, a point down there. Can Revolution do printer lights?
a: Not as step keys yet (a gap). The same move by hand: the Offset wheel on the balance node (`grade.wheel.offset`); under it the red, green and blue boxes take typed values, so type the same small step per channel each time. In a log working space Offset moves the whole picture evenly, like a printer light. To carry one trim to many shots there are no shared nodes yet: keep the trim as the only node of one reference clip, Copy Grade (`grade.copy`), select the shots and Append Grade (`grade.append`), which keeps their own nodes and adds the trim after them. If you change the trim, append it again.

q: whole film is a tad green, want to nudge every shot by the same amount
a: Make the nudge once, on a reference clip whose grade is only that one node (a spare copy of any shot): Offset (`grade.wheel.offset`) a small step away from green (type it in the green box under the wheel, or pull Tint slightly to magenta). Copy that grade (`grade.copy`; it copies every node of the clip, hence the one-node reference), select the other clips and Append Grade (`grade.append`): each keeps its own grade and gets the same nudge on top. There are no shared nodes yet, so a later change means appending again; Check scene in the Match tab (`grade.checkScene`) then shows any shot that still stands out.
